It is worth noting that, after the corrosion allowance has been taken into account, the wall thickness of the absorber comes to 63 mm. This figure matters because the corrosion allowance essentially represents metal that is expected to be gradually consumed over the service life of the vessel, which means that the pressure integrity of the absorber ultimately rests on the corroded thickness rather than on the thickness of the shell as originally fabricated. A design that relied on the uncorroded thickness would start out compliant but would slowly move away from compliance as corrosion progressed over the years.

When it comes to the gasket materials for the flange joints, the comparison between the two candidate materials rests solely on temperature limit. Both materials are capable of sealing the joint at the design pressure, so the decisive consideration is the temperature that each material can withstand at the joint face. On that basis, the higher-rated material is preferred, since a gasket that performs perfectly well at ambient temperature but softens at operating temperature can lose bolt load as the joint heats up, potentially leading to leakage at the flange face over time.

target:
Wall thickness for the absorber comes to 63 mm after the corrosion allowance is added. The allowance is not a margin on the pressure calculation; it is metal given up to corrosion over the vessel life, and the pressure case is checked on the corroded thickness, not on the thickness as fabricated. A shell sized on the uncorroded figure would meet the pressure requirement on delivery and lose it as corrosion proceeds, so the stated thickness is the figure the rest of the design must use.

Gasket selection for the flange joints on the absorber turns on temperature limit alone. Two materials are under consideration, and each seals the joint at the design pressure; the difference between them is the temperature each can withstand at the joint face. The higher-rated material is preferred. A gasket that seals at ambient conditions but softens at operating temperature loses bolt load as the joint heats, and the joint then weeps at the flange face; rating the gasket for the operating temperature removes that failure mode rather than managing it by retightening.

The lean solvent pump takes suction from the absorber sump, and its available NPSH falls as the liquid level in the sump falls. $\Delta P$ through the suction line rises with flow, so the level at which the pump can still draw solvent without cavitation depends on the operating point the absorber is run at.
